title: Food Creator Membership Platform: How to Pick and Launch
summary: Pick a food creator membership platform: what members pay for, Patreon vs Substack vs beehiiv fees, simple tiers, launching to followers and churn.
body_markdown:
A food creator membership platform turns your most loyal followers into steady monthly income. Brand deals come and go, and ad income moves with the seasons, but a member who pays every month gives you a base to plan around.


Our point of view: sell time saved, not "exclusive content". Food fans join for a meal plan that answers "what's for dinner", not for a vague promise of extras. Start from the problem your members want solved.


## What do food members pay for?


Food members pay for things that save time or feel personal. The most common benefits:


-


**Weekly meal plans**


with a shopping list, so the week is decided.


-


**Members-only recipes**


, especially the ones followers keep asking for.


-


**Early access**


to new recipes before they go public.


-


**Ad-free reading**


of your recipe archive.


-


**Live cook-alongs**


or Q&A sessions.


-


**Direct questions**


, such as substitutions or troubleshooting.


Pick one main benefit and do it well. A meal plan delivered every Sunday is worth more than six benefits delivered when you remember.


## Food creator membership platform options compared


Choose the platform based on where your members will actually spend time. Fees matter, but a platform members never open will lose them.


Platform


Fee on member income


Best for


Patreon


10%, plus processing, conversion and payout fees


A separate members' space with tiers and community


Substack


10% of paid subscriptions, plus Stripe fees


Members who mainly want recipes by email


beehiiv


0% on paid plans, plus Stripe fees


Email memberships at larger list sizes


Sources:


[Patreon pricing](https://www.patreon.com/pricing)


,


[Substack's pricing help page](https://support.substack.com/hc/en-us/articles/360037607131-How-much-does-Substack-cost)


and


[beehiiv pricing](https://www.beehiiv.com/pricing)


. Note that beehiiv's paid subscription tools need a paid plan. Check each page before you decide, since terms change.


## Pricing tiers that work


Two or three tiers are enough. More than that and people stall trying to compare.


Tier


What it includes


Who it's for


Supporter


A thank-you, early access to new recipes


Fans who want to back your work


Main


Weekly meal plan, members-only recipes


Most members


Kitchen table


Everything above, plus live sessions or Q&A


Your most engaged fans


Price the main tier around the benefit, not your follower count. Ask yourself what a week of planned dinners is worth to a busy reader, then test it. Our guide to

can help you see which audiences tend to pay for planning help.

## Launching to your existing followers


Your first members come from people who already engage with you. A simple launch plan:


1.


Ask in Stories what followers would pay for, using a poll with two or three options.


2.


Build a small founding offer around the top answer.


3.


Open a waitlist and share a preview, such as one sample meal plan.


4.


Launch on a set date with a founding price for the first month.


5.


Post member results, with permission, such as a reader cooking the plan.


Launch with enough content ready for the first month. Running behind in week two is the fastest way to lose new members.


## Churn and retention


Churn is the share of members who cancel. You can't stop it entirely, but you can slow it.


-


**Keep a fixed schedule.**


Members should know exactly when the next plan arrives.


-


**Welcome new members well.**


Send your best recipes and a short guide to the archive in the first week.


-


**Show the value.**


A monthly recap of what members got makes the price easy to justify.


-


**Ask leavers why.**


One question on cancel tells you what to fix.


## Where memberships fit with other income


A membership works best on top of other streams, not instead of them. Most followers will never pay monthly, so recipe pages, grocery commissions and brand deals still earn from everyone else. See
